name: The bad day: reliability ops
note: Three moments from an incident. For each, pick the reliability tool that fits — before the chapter names SLOs, degradation modes, and runbooks.

items.prompt: Leadership wants 'zero incidents' as the reliability target for the bot, and the team is told to stop shipping until that's guaranteed.
candidates: Set an SLO with an error budget instead — e.g. 99.9% of requests good — so the allowed failure is an explicit budget you spend on shipping velocity; 'zero incidents' is not a target, it's a way to stop improving
Agree — zero incidents is the only acceptable standard for production
SLOs are for infra uptime and don't apply to AI quality
Promise 100% and add more reviewers to every change
items.correct: Set an SLO with an error budget instead — e.g. 99.9% of requests good — so the allowed failure is an explicit budget you spend on shipping velocity; 'zero incidents' is not a target, it's a way to stop improving
items.explanation: Reliability is a budget, not an absolute. An SLO (a target like 99.9% good) implies an error budget — the failures you're allowed — and the budget is what you spend to ship at all. 'Zero incidents' either halts delivery or quietly gets violated and ignored. And SLOs apply to *quality* for AI systems (groundedness, refusal rate), not just uptime — that's the fourth-pillar point from Chapter 5.
items.principle: An SLO with an error budget makes reliability a number you manage; 'zero incidents' just stops the line.

items.prompt: The model provider has a regional outage. Right now, every request to the bot times out and returns a 500.
candidates: Define a degradation mode: fall back to a cached answer, a cheaper backup model, or an honest 'I can't answer that right now' — so an upstream outage degrades gracefully instead of hard-failing every request
Wait for the provider to recover; outages are their responsibility
Retry the failing call in a tight loop until it succeeds
Show the raw 500 error to users so they know it's not your fault
items.correct: Define a degradation mode: fall back to a cached answer, a cheaper backup model, or an honest 'I can't answer that right now' — so an upstream outage degrades gracefully instead of hard-failing every request
items.explanation: Resilience is planning the bad day in advance. A degradation mode is the fallback from Chapter 1, now a reliability control: when the primary path fails, serve something safe and useful — a cached response, a backup model, or a graceful 'try later.' Tight retries make an overloaded provider worse (a thundering herd); showing 500s is the hard failure you were trying to avoid.
items.principle: Plan the degradation: an upstream outage should drop you to a safe fallback, not a wall of 500s.

items.prompt: A quality alert fires at 3 a.m. The on-call engineer has never seen this failure and doesn't know whether to roll back, flip a flag, or page someone.
candidates: Write a runbook: for each known alert, a tested procedure — what it means, how to mitigate now (flip the kill switch / roll back), and who to escalate to — so a 3 a.m. incident is a checklist, not improvisation
Hire more senior engineers so on-call always knows what to do
Add more alerts so the problem is more visible
Tell on-call to wait until business hours to investigate
items.correct: Write a runbook: for each known alert, a tested procedure — what it means, how to mitigate now (flip the kill switch / roll back), and who to escalate to — so a 3 a.m. incident is a checklist, not improvisation
items.explanation: A runbook converts tribal knowledge into a procedure anyone on-call can execute under stress. The first step is usually the kill switch / feature flag from Chapter 1 (mitigate first, debug later), then a known-good rollback, then escalation. More alerts without runbooks is more 3 a.m. panic; better hiring doesn't scale to every failure class. The runbook is what makes the response repeatable.
items.principle: A runbook turns a 3 a.m. unknown into a tested checklist: mitigate (flag/rollback) first, then escalate.
